Chester-le-Street.region: Chester-le-Street and the Vale of Durham
Chester-le-Street.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of Durham
s1loc: Chester-le-Street built its visitor draw on the River Wear, and its marquee venue is the Seat Unique Riverside, home of Durham County Cricket Club, where international and county fixtures and big-name concerts from Elton John to Diana Ross fill the stands below Lumley Castle. The 14th-century castle itself, now a four-star hotel and event venue, commands the Wear valley and anchors the old market town's headline appeal.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Riverside Park along the Wear, with its artist-designed ornamental gardens, events arena, paddling pool and play area drawing families through the warmer months. The world-famous Beamish open-air museum, a short drive west, recreates the 1820s Pockerley, the 1900s pit village and the 1940s farm, and its trams and steam keep operators busy across the season around the town.

Heritage and culture run through the ancient Tuesday, Friday and Saturday market, one of the oldest in the North East, and the Anker's House Museum beside the parish church of St Mary and St Cuthbert, where the body of St Cuthbert once rested. The Roman fort of Concangis lies beneath the town, and the Lambton Estate and its parkland add a year-round events draw nearby.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base led by Lumley Castle and a guide scene built around the cricket, the museum and the river walks. Chester-le-Street railway station on the East Coast Main Line links Durham, Newcastle and the south, and the A1(M) puts the Angel of the North at Gateshead and the wider Durham coast within an easy day trip, feeding a steady seasonal flow.

Wednesbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Black Country
s1loc: Wednesbury anchors a Black Country visitor draw led by its purpose-built Victorian Wednesbury Museum and Art Gallery on Holyhead Road, home to one of the world's largest collections of Ruskin pottery alongside Pre-Raphaelite works and a room devoted to Chance Brothers of Smethwick, who glazed the Crystal Palace and the clock faces of Big Ben. The old hilltop St Bartholomew's Church crowns the market town's skyline.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into Sandwell Valley Country Park, over 1,800 acres of open countryside with Forge Mill Farm and its rare breeds, the RSPB reserve on Forge Mill Lake, high ropes, an adventure playground and cycle trails. The restored Victorian Sandwell Park Farm with its walled kitchen gardens adds to a green belt that keeps families and walkers busy across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Black Country Living Museum at neighbouring Dudley, an open-air recreation of rebuilt shops and houses with electric trams, trolleybuses and narrowboat trips into the Dudley Tunnel, and the town's ancient three-day market keeps its trading past alive. Wednesbury Museum carries a lively events calendar of talks, live music and theatre through the year.

The visitor trade leans on a roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the country park and the museum trail, with the West Midlands Metro tram running from Wednesbury through to Wolverhampton and Birmingham and a new line under construction to Dudley town centre. The M6 and M5 junctions put Walsall, Tipton and the wider Black Country geopark within easy reach, feeding a steady day-trip flow.

Denton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Tameside
s1loc: Denton built its identity on the felt-hatting trade, once the third largest hat-making centre in the north west with twenty-five firms working by the 1820s, a past marked by the beaver on its coat of arms and told at the timber-framed St Lawrence's Church on Town Lane, a rare medieval survival founded as a chapel of ease in 1531 and the town's headline heritage landmark.

The leisure and activity layer rises to Werneth Low Country Park on the hill that dominates the southern boundary, with panoramic views over Manchester and the Cheshire Plain, walking trails and the war memorial. Victoria Park, opened in 1913 with its restored bandstand, and the reservoirs and woodland paths of Debdale and the Tame valley give families and walkers green space through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Portland Basin Museum at the canal junction in neighbouring Ashton-under-Lyne, where the Ashton, Peak Forest and Huddersfield Narrow canals meet, and the Museum of the Manchesters and Setantii gallery telling Tameside's story. Denton Local History Society and St Lawrence's hatting exhibition keep the town's distinctive trade and events calendar alive across the year.

The visitor trade leans on a roadside hotel base around the M60 and a guide scene built around the canals and the country park, with Crown Point shopping park and Crown Point North on the site of the old Wilton Street hatting quarter drawing retail crowds. The motorway and the Manchester tram network at nearby Droylsden put the city and the Peak District fringe within an easy day trip.

Port Talbot.region: Port Talbot and the Neath Port Talbot coast
Port Talbot.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Neath Port Talbot coast
s1loc: Port Talbot built its visitor draw on the three-mile sweep of Aberavon Beach at Sandfields, a long sandy seafront popular for swimming, kayaking, sand yachting and kitesurfing, with a promenade carrying the Celtic Trail cycle route, a Ferris wheel and a small waterpark. The marquee inland anchor is Margam Country Park, 1,000 acres of parkland around the Gothic-revival Margam Castle and the largest deer herd in Wales.

The leisure and activity layer spreads from the seafront aqua splash, skate park and adventure golf to the Afan Forest Park, which holds more all-weather mountain-bike singletrack than any other centre in Wales with six flowing trails and an extreme bike park. Go Ape at Margam runs a high-ropes course with zip wires up to 180 metres, keeping activity operators busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the South Wales Miners Museum within Afan Forest Park, where ex-miners share the underground story, and the medieval ruins and orangery of the Margam estate. Margam Abbey and its Cistercian past, the town's steel-making heritage and a busy seafront events calendar along the Aberavon promenade give the area a year-round cultural pull alongside the open coast.

The visitor trade leans on a seafront and town hotel base and a guide scene built around the beach, the country park and the forest trails. Port Talbot Parkway station on the South Wales Main Line links Swansea, Cardiff and the west, and the M4 corridor puts Neath, Bridgend and the Maesteg valley within easy reach, feeding a strong seasonal flow along the Swansea Bay coast.

Aldershot.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Aldershot garrison town
s1loc: Aldershot grew up around the camp founded in 1854 as the first permanent training base in Britain, and the Home of the British Army still frames its appeal. The Aldershot Military Museum, housed in the only surviving Victorian brick barracks, tells the garrison story through uniforms and vehicles, while the 30-foot bronze Iron Duke statue by Matthew Cotes Wyatt, moved here from Hyde Park Corner in 1884, stands as the town's marquee landmark on Round Hill.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Manor Park, a public park since 1919 with its spring-fed pond, and Aldershot Park near the town centre, alongside the 200-acre Aldershot Garrison Sports Centre offering football, rugby, athletics, cricket and hockey. The Recreation Ground, home of Aldershot Town and known as The Rec, draws fixture crowds, and the wooded heaths and trails around the town keep families and walkers busy across the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Princes Hall in the town centre, the 600-seat theatre opened by Prince Philip in 1973 that carries music, ballet, comedy and pantomime through the year. The garrison church, the Victorian barracks streets and the military events calendar give the town a distinctive character, with the Royal Garrison and its parades a draw for visitors interested in army heritage.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the military museum and the garrison, with Aldershot railway station on the line from Waterloo and the M3 and A31 close by. The nearby Farnborough airfield and its air shows, the historic market town of Farnham and Camberley put a wide day-trip and seasonal draw within easy reach across north east Hampshire and Surrey.

Airdrie.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Monklands
s1loc: Airdrie sits on a plateau twelve miles east of Glasgow, and its standout draw is the Airdrie Public Observatory, one of only four public observatories in the United Kingdom, established in 1896 and housed within Airdrie Library on Wellwynd. The grand sandstone Airdrie Town Hall anchors the market-town centre, and the Summerlee Museum of Scottish Industrial Life at neighbouring Coatbridge is one of Scotland's top free attractions.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Drumpellier Country Park, a sweep of woodlands, lochs and walking and cycling routes popular for birdwatching, and on Centenary Park and the town's green spaces. Summerlee runs a recreated mine, historic tram rides and hands-on industrial machinery, and the loch and woodland trails around the Monklands keep families and walkers busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the Monkland Canal, where the Vulcan, the world's first iron boat, was built and launched in 1819, with its towpath now part of the Summerlee and Drumpellier route. The town traces its name to the Cistercian monks of Newbattle Abbey and grew on weaving, coal and manufacturing, a past told at Summerlee and carried through a year-round events calendar at the town hall.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the museum, the observatory and the country park. Airdrie railway station runs frequent trains to Glasgow via Coatbridge and, since the Airdrie to Bathgate line reopened in 2010, direct to Livingston and Edinburgh Waverley, putting Motherwell, Cumbernauld and both Scottish cities within an easy day trip.

Accrington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Hyndburn
s1loc: Accrington's marquee draw is the Haworth Art Gallery, a Tudor-style mansion of 1909 designed by Walter Brierley that holds the largest collection of Louis Comfort Tiffany glass in Europe, some 140 pieces gifted by Accrington-born Tiffany designer Joseph Briggs. Set in landscaped grounds above the town, the gallery and its artists' studios anchor the visitor appeal of the old Lancashire cotton town in the Hyndburn valley.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Peel Park and the Coppice, the hillside parkland and reservoir lodges given to the town by the Peel family and opened in 1909 with a procession of 5,000 schoolchildren. Oswaldtwistle Mills, a visitor attraction in a former cotton mill nearby, blends a textiles heritage centre with craft and gift shops, and the moorland trails above the town draw walkers across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the town's hard-wearing Accrington Nori brick, used worldwide, and the Accrington Pals story of the First World War, told around the town. Accrington Stanley, a founder member of the Football League in 1888, draws fixture crowds to the Wham Stadium, where a heritage mural on the Crown pub marks the club and the town's mill-chimney industrial past.

The visitor trade leans on a town hotel base and a guide scene built around the gallery, the parks and the mills, with the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the Pennine moors on the doorstep. Accrington railway station on the East Lancashire line links Blackburn, Burnley and Manchester, and the heritage East Lancashire Railway at nearby Rawtenstall adds to a steady day-trip and seasonal flow through the valley.
